q: The back office renders <p>{review.body}</p>, and the body is <img src=x onerror="steal()">. What does React 19 produce?
options: An <img> element whose onerror runs when the image fails to load
A render error, because React refuses text that contains HTML
The payload as text inside the paragraph, with < encoded
An <img> element whose onerror attribute React removed before insertion
explain: A value between braces is text: react-dom/server encoded it as <img … onerror="…, and react-dom/client inserted a text node (measured with 19.3.1). React does not strip attributes from user HTML because it never parses it as HTML in the first place; that would be a sanitiser's job.

q: A customer saves a review containing a script payload, and it runs later in the browser of every agent who opens the order. Which kind of XSS is it?
options: Stored XSS
Reflected XSS
DOM-based XSS only
Clickjacking
explain: The payload is saved on the server and served to other users later: that is stored XSS. Reflected XSS travels in the request (a URL parameter) and comes back in the immediate response. The sink here happens to be in the front end, but what defines the kind is where the payload lives.

q: React 19.3 renders <a href="javascript:alert(1)">site</a>. What is in the DOM?
options: The same href; React only logs a warning in development builds
An anchor with no href attribute at all
Nothing: rendering throws and the component does not mount
An href React swaps for a javascript: URL that throws an error
explain: React 19 swaps the URL for javascript:throw new Error('React has blocked a javascript: URL as a security precaution.'), in both the development and production builds of react-dom 19.3.1 (measured on the server and in Chromium, where clicking the link threw instead of running the code). Nothing is removed, and rendering does not fail.

q: Which of these is not covered by React's automatic encoding?
options: A string rendered as a child: {review.body}
The __html value of dangerouslySetInnerHTML
A string in a title attribute
A string in a data-review-id attribute on the card
explain: dangerouslySetInnerHTML is the explicit escape hatch: its string is inserted as HTML, as is (measured: the <img onerror> came out intact). Text children and attribute values are encoded, which is why the other three are safe.

q: Product insists that reviews keep bold, italics and lists. Which technique makes rendering that HTML safe?
options: Sanitisation with an allow-list, right before the HTML sink
Validation with a regular expression at the API boundary, before saving
Output encoding of the whole review before rendering
A Content Security Policy instead of any change to the code
explain: Only a sanitiser keeps the allowed formatting while removing everything else. Encoding the whole review would display the tags as text, which defeats the requirement, and validation cannot decide what is safe HTML in every context. CSP is a second layer, not the fix.

q: Why does the team sanitise reviews in the component that renders them, rather than only once before saving?
options: Because DOMPurify cannot run in Node, so the API could not call it before saving
Because storing sanitised HTML breaks database indexes
Because safety depends on the final string at the sink, and later edits can undo it
Because sanitising twice would double-encode the text
explain: The DOMPurify README warns that modifying HTML after sanitising can void it, and the allow-list may change after the data was stored. Sanitising at the sink checks the exact string that reaches the browser. DOMPurify does run in Node, given a jsdom window.

q: A page is served with Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-abc123'. Which of these run?
options: All three: the policy only applies to external scripts
The nonced script and the onerror handler
None: a nonce only works in a meta tag
Only the nonced script
explain: Measured in Chromium: the inline script and the inline event handler were both blocked ("Executing inline event handler violates…"), and only the nonced script ran. That is exactly why a CSP would have stopped the review's onerror payload.

q: What does 'strict-dynamic' change in a nonce-based policy?
options: It lets inline scripts run without a nonce, as long as the parser inserted them
Scripts loaded by a nonced script are trusted; host lists are ignored
It forces every script to load with async
It restricts scripts to the page's own origin
explain: MDN: trust given by a nonce or hash propagates to scripts that root script loads, and allow-lists or 'self' are ignored. Measured: a script appended by the nonced loader ran, while a parser-inserted script from a listed host was blocked.

q: The back office sends require-trusted-types-for 'script'. What happens on element.innerHTML = '<b>x</b>'?
options: It works, and the browser logs a Trusted Types warning in the console
The assignment is silently ignored
It throws a TypeError: the document requires TrustedHTML
The browser sanitises the string automatically
explain: Measured in Chromium: "TypeError: Failed to set the 'innerHTML' property on 'Element': This document requires 'TrustedHTML' assignment." The browser does not sanitise; you supply a policy that does. A warning without blocking is what the report-only header gives.

q: An XSS runs on the storefront. Compare a refresh token in localStorage with a session held behind an HttpOnly cookie by a BFF.
options: The token can be copied and replayed elsewhere; the cookie cannot be read
Both are equally exposed: an injected script can read the cookie and the token alike
Both are safe: same-origin policy keeps scripts away from both
The cookie is worse, because fetch sends it to any site the script calls
explain: Web storage is readable by any script of the origin, so the token leaves with the attacker. HttpOnly forbids reading the cookie, but the browser still attaches it to requests from the infected page, so XSS prevention still comes first. And fetch attaches a cookie only to requests for the host that set it, not to any site the script calls.

q: What does CORS control?
options: Whether the server accepts and runs a request coming from another origin
Whether the browser attaches cookies to a request
Whether the caller is authorised to perform the action
Whether a script from another origin may read the response
explain: CORS relaxes the same-origin policy on reading. In every measurement of section 7, the server received and ran the request whatever the Origin. Cookie attachment is SameSite's job, and authorisation is the server's.

q: A Vite app's .env contains VITE_PAYMENT_SECRET=sk_live_oops, used in client code. What does vite build do with it?
options: It refuses to build because the value looks like a secret
It inlines the value as plain text in the JavaScript bundle
It encrypts the value with a per-build key that only the page can read
It exposes the value only in the development server
explain: Measured with Vite 8.3.4: the bundle contained 'sk_live_oops' as a string literal, while an unprefixed variable became void 0. Vite's docs say VITE_* variables should not contain sensitive information such as API keys.

q: A server-rendered search page embeds the query for hydration. The URL is ?q=</script><script>steal()</script>. What happens in the browser?
options: The query closes the script element early and the attacker's script runs
JSON.stringify escapes the angle brackets, so the query stays a harmless string
React encodes the __html of a script element, so nothing runs
The browser parses the JSON first, so the query stays a string
explain: The HTML parser ends a script element at the first </script>, before any JavaScript is parsed, and JSON.stringify does not escape <. Measured in Chromium: the injected script ran and window.__SEARCH__ was never set. Replacing < with \u003c fixed it.

q: Reviews have an optional "unboxing video" URL rendered as <a href={videoUrl}>. Which fix would you ship?
options: Wrap it in encodeURIComponent(videoUrl) before passing it to href
Nothing: React 19 already blocks dangerous URLs
Parse it with URL and allow only https: and http:
Remove the substring javascript: with a replace
explain: Parsing and allow-listing the protocol rejects javascript: with any casing, spacing or tab, and data: URLs too (measured on Node 24). React blocks only javascript:, so data: passes; encodeURIComponent breaks valid URLs; and a substring replace misses java\tscript:.

q: A colleague proposes to sanitise review HTML with html.replace(/<script[\s\S]*?<\/script>/gi, ''). Why do you reject it?
options: Regular expressions are too slow for 5,000-character reviews
Payloads need no script tag: onerror handlers and javascript: URLs pass a deny-list
It is unnecessary, because browsers never run any HTML that is inserted with innerHTML
Regular expressions cannot match Unicode characters
explain: Scripts inserted with innerHTML do not run, which is precisely why attackers use <img onerror> and similar. A deny-list must predict every vector; an allow-list sanitiser such as DOMPurify keeps only known-safe elements and attributes. The third option is half true and dangerous: other HTML inserted that way does run handlers.

q: The storefront has never had a CSP and loads several third-party scripts. What do you ship first?
options: An enforced strict CSP for 10% of users, then for everyone a week later
An enforced policy with 'unsafe-inline' so nothing breaks
A CSP in a meta tag, to avoid touching the server
The strict policy as Report-Only with a report endpoint, then enforce
explain: Report-only lets everything run and reports each violation (measured: Chromium POSTed an application/csp-report with "disposition":"report"). Even 10% enforced breaks real checkouts, and 'unsafe-inline' without a nonce gives up the main protection against injected inline scripts.

q: Which scripts run under script-src 'nonce-r4nd' 'strict-dynamic' https://cdn.shop.example?
code:
<!-- loader.js appends <script src="https://cdn.shop.example/chat.js"> with createElement -->
<script nonce="r4nd" src="/loader.js"></script>
<script src="https://cdn.shop.example/widget.js"></script>
options: loader.js and chat.js; widget.js is blocked
All three: the CDN host is listed in the policy, so its scripts are allowed
Only loader.js
loader.js and widget.js; chat.js is blocked
explain: With 'strict-dynamic', the nonced loader is trusted and so are scripts it creates, while host allow-lists are ignored. Measured in Chromium: the appended script ran, and the parser-inserted script from the listed host was blocked with "host-based allowlisting is disabled".

q: The storefront's product pages are statically generated with ISR. The team adds a nonce-based CSP in proxy.ts. What must they accept?
options: Nothing changes: Next.js writes a fresh nonce into each static page at build time
Nonces work only with the development server
Dynamic rendering: no static generation, ISR or CDN caching of the HTML
Next.js generates one nonce per build and reuses it
explain: The Next.js CSP guide says nonces require dynamic rendering: a static page is built when no request exists, so it cannot carry a per-request nonce, and Partial Prerendering is incompatible. A nonce reused across responses would be guessable. For static pages, the guide offers the experimental SRI option.

q: The back office enforces Trusted Types and runs React 19.3.1. A developer writes <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: '<b>x</b>' }} />. What happens?
options: React sanitises the string because Trusted Types are on
React converts the string to TrustedHTML on its own
It renders, because React writes HTML through an API outside Trusted Types
The commit throws a TypeError, reported to onUncaughtError; nothing renders
explain: Measured in Chromium: the root stayed empty and onUncaughtError received "This document requires 'TrustedHTML' assignment". React passes values through since 19.3, so a plain string reaches the sink and is refused; only an object from a policy is accepted.

q: The CSP says require-trusted-types-for 'script'; trusted-types review-html. A library calls the code below. What happens?
options: It is created: the directive only limits how many policies a page may create
createPolicy throws, because the name is not listed in trusted-types
It is created, but the browser rejects its output
It is created in report-only mode
explain: Measured in Chromium: "Policy "passthrough" disallowed". Listing policy names is what keeps a library from adding a policy that returns its input unchanged, which would defeat enforcement. Review each listed policy like security code.

q: An agent logs in; the BFF sets a cookie with no SameSite attribute. Thirty seconds later, the agent opens a page on evil.example that auto-submits a form POST to the back office. What does Chromium do?
options: Sends it: Lax by default still allows a top-level POST for 2 minutes
Withholds it: without the attribute, Chromium applies SameSite=Strict to every request
Sends the cookie: without the attribute, Chromium applies None
Rejects the cookie at login because it has no SameSite attribute
explain: Measured: the cookie was sent on the cross-site POST right after login, and not sent after 125 seconds, when plain Lax applied. A Lax default with that 2-minute exception is why you set SameSite explicitly. Chromium treats the missing attribute as Lax, not None.

q: An XSS runs on www.shop.example. It calls fetch('https://backoffice.shop.example/api/me', { credentials: 'include' }), and the back office cookie is SameSite=Strict. Is the cookie sent?
options: No: Strict blocks every cross-origin request
No: HttpOnly cookies are never sent by fetch
Yes: both hosts are the same site, so SameSite does not apply
Only if the back office answers the preflight with CORS headers allowing it
explain: SameSite compares sites (shop.example), not origins. Measured: the Strict cookie was attached, and the server received it even when it sent no CORS headers; CORS only decided whether the script could read the answer. That is why the BFF rejects Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site on state changes.

q: In code review you find this BFF setting, and the session cookie is SameSite=None; Secure. What is the impact?
options: None: SameSite=None still blocks cross-site requests
Any site the agent visits can read the agent's API responses
Nothing: browsers refuse to honour a reflected origin when credentials are included
Only preflighted requests are affected
explain: Measured: a script on evil.example fetched /api/me with credentials and read the JSON, cookie included. Reflecting Origin with credentials allows every origin to read; use an exact allow-list, or no CORS at all for a same-origin SPA. SameSite=None is precisely the setting that allows cross-site sending.

q: An API answers Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. A script on another origin calls it with credentials: 'include'. What happens?
options: It works: the cookies are sent and the response is readable
The browser strips the cookies and lets the script read the response
The server receives nothing: the browser cancels the request
The browser hides the response: * is not allowed with credentials
explain: Measured in Chromium: fetch rejected with "Failed to fetch" and the console said the header "must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'". The request itself still reached the server (measured); only the reading was blocked, so this misconfiguration fails safe but breaks the feature.

q: The BFF's cookie is SameSite=None. Which request from evil.example reaches POST /orders/ord_a1/refund with the cookie, without a preflight?
options: fetch(url, { method: 'POST', mode: 'no-cors', credentials: 'include', body: '{"amountCents":999}' })
fetch(url, { method: 'POST', credentials: 'include', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' } })
fetch(url, { method: 'POST', credentials: 'include', headers: { 'x-requested-by': 'backoffice' } })
fetch(url, { method: 'PUT', credentials: 'include', body: '{"amountCents":999}' })
explain: A no-cors POST with a string body is sent as text/plain, a "simple" request, so no preflight (measured: the server saw the POST with the cookie). JSON, custom headers and PUT trigger an OPTIONS preflight, and since the BFF approved nothing, the real request never left. That is why the BFF requires application/json.

q: With the isAllowedStateChange guard of section 7, what does this call return?
options: true, because same-site requests come from one of the shop's own subdomains
true, because a JSON body cannot be forged cross-site
false: only same-origin passes when Sec-Fetch-Site is present
It throws, because the origin is not in the allow-list
explain: The guard accepts a state change only when Sec-Fetch-Site is same-origin, and falls back to the Origin list only when the header is missing (run on Node 24: false). Accepting same-site would let an XSS on the storefront issue refunds through the back office.

q: In the storefront, a Client Component calls a helper that reads process.env.SEARCH_ADMIN_KEY (no prefix). The helper does not import server-only. What happens in the browser?
options: The admin key is inlined in the client bundle as a plain string literal
The build fails with an environment error
Next.js fetches the value from the server at runtime
The reference is replaced with an empty string, so the call fails
explain: The Next.js docs: only NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are included in the client bundle, and others are replaced with an empty string. Nothing leaks, but the bug is silent; importing server-only in the helper turns it into a build-time error.

q: A legacy back office page sends X-Frame-Options: DENY and Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors *. A site on another origin frames it. What does Chromium do?
options: Frames it: frame-ancestors takes precedence over X-Frame-Options
Blocks it: X-Frame-Options always wins
Blocks it: framing is allowed only when both headers agree that it is allowed
Frames it only for same-origin parents
explain: Measured in Chromium: the page loaded inside the frame of the other origin. When frame-ancestors is present, X-Frame-Options is ignored, so a permissive CSP silently cancels a strict X-Frame-Options. Set both consistently.

q: What is the bug in this checkout listener?
options: It should check event.source only, because the origin string can be spoofed
includes accepts origins like https://pay.example.evil.example
event.origin is always "null" for messages from iframes
postMessage data is always a string, so event.data.type is always undefined
explain: The origin is set by the browser and cannot be spoofed, but a substring test accepts any host containing the text. Compare with !== against the exact origin, check event.source too, and validate the data with a schema. Measured: a cross-origin frame's message arrived as an object with an origin like https://pay.example.

q: A page loads <script src="https://cdn.reviews-widget.example/widget.js" integrity="sha384-…"> without a crossorigin attribute. The CDN does send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. What happens?
options: The script runs, and its integrity is checked
The script runs, but the integrity check is skipped because CORS is missing
Blocked: integrity needs a CORS request, so crossorigin is required
The script runs, with a console warning only
explain: Measured in Chromium: "the resource requires the request to be CORS enabled to check the integrity, and it is not. The resource has been blocked." The CDN's header is not enough; the tag must ask for CORS with crossorigin="anonymous". Browsers fail closed rather than run an unchecked file.
